utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: For witness protection reasons can we just go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are we in private session?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your cousin, Dragan Vinac, tell us about him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know a Mr. Dragan Vinac, and he's a distant relative. He's not my cousin or a close relative. All I can say is that we went to school together when we were children. He currently lives in Vitez. He's not in the village. That's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his connection to the Vitezovi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know that he was with Vitezovi, but what was his duty, his rank there, I really don't know and I really wasn't interested, because I was simply too busy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he the deputy to Kraljevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really don't know, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he there, to your knowledge, on the night of the 15th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, according to stories, I think he was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you mean "according to stories"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, like that; there was a lot of argument. That is, I guess. I suppose so. I wasn't that night in the cafe and I did not hear it from anyone that he was there. Those are family conversations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. Please explain. "According to stories I think he was not." Does that mean that right at the time there were discussions amongst you and your fellow Croats that he was there on the night of the 15th; this was something being discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, we did not talk about anything, because there was no need to. That night, on the 15th of April, was not [sic] in the bar. I worked until half past 6.00, and I really -- I mean, I don't know. I think, according to stories in the family of late, here and there, when I had something, at least in my family, we talked, and I suppose I think he was not, but I really don't know [as interpreted]. I cannot affirm that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One last question on that. How would the absence of somebody unimportant ever be dealt with in the informal stories told in your family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand, Your Honours. Could you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I didn't understand it either. Yes. Can we move along, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. We are coming towards the end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the position is this, isn't it, that you know full well that Mr. Kordic visited your village on more than one occasion, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Kordic was never in my village, never; at least, I don't know of it. I really don't know anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before I end, just two matters of detail. You accept, don't you, that your injury on the 17th of April of 1993 at Donja Veceriska will be recorded as an injury suffered by a member of the Viteska Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exhibit 957.1, for reference.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You accept that that's how your injury will be recorded, don't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this was an administrative error. The Vitez Brigade, or rather company, kept a record of all the killed, of all the wounded members, and it must have simply happened that it was recorded like that. But that was an error. I was never a member of the Vitez Brigade. Between February 1992, I was with the Mio Centre, and there I was engaged in air surveillance, an area of Vares, Zepce, and to protect the territory from Serb aircraft; defended industry; installations; and I therefore never was a member of the Vitez Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course we've heard that to some degree these brigades acted with people who were at home some of the time and fighting some of the time. You'd accept that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Your Honours, I did not really understand this. Could you repeat this?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because the Court is pressed for time, I'm going to conclude this single topic in this way: The reason you're recorded as injured in the Viteska Brigade on the night of the 15th, 16th, 17th -- I beg your pardon, on the 17th, is because you were part of the plan to attack your own village's Muslims and you did so; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is not correct. I was not a member of the Vitez Brigade, nor was there any plan to attack Muslims. I really know nothing about that plan. I told you yesterday that that night, on the 15th of April, asked the man on duty, I had asked him about the situation, and was told that it was normal, and I really did not know about any plan, about any conflict with Muslims, with our neighbours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wish to ask this witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, can you help us? What page of 957.1 can we find the entry?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 957.1, his name appears on I think it's page 3, wounded, number 16. It has it there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I think it's part of the same exhibit. One goes on several pages to ERN 00807836. You can find his name again also listed at number 16. To conclude, I wish to ask this witness one question about a document recently presented. It's outside the scope of the general topic, but I would like his assistance, with your leave. And the document is 1466.2. If the document could be handed to me first, 1466.2. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a document, as you can see, Mr. Vinac, that has your name on it and a signature. Can you just tell us what the document is? Having seen where your name and signature is, you can look at the rest of the document, by all means.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. We did not get the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was my first rank. That was my rank. The first rank that I was awarded is rank of a lieutenant, and that is true, but this is not my signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, can you explain how a document like this, which comes from, I think, records of your unit, comes into existence? What sort of a document is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really don't know, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just remind us. It's headed, I think, with -- at the front of the first page, with -- I'll just get a translation. Headed with -- the heading of the list is what? You tell us. Just read it out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, it says "Military District Vitez".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And therefore it's got a list of office holders. Can you explain, please, why the third name down from the top is Kordic, with a signature? Can you explain that to us, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, as for this signature and this document and this name under number 3, Dario -- father's name, Pero Kordic, I would not comment on that. I heard that the gentleman had a rank, but I know that the gentleman was a politician. He was not involved in the military. He did not give orders to anyone, at least not to my knowledge. That's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't want to debate the general topic with you; I only wanted your help with the document. And you can't just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: While we're on the document, it appears to be -- perhaps you can help us with this, Mr. Vinac. It appears to be a document, as I recollect it, where the individuals on it are signing for insignia. Does that appear to be what it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, indeed I don't know, because here on page 2 -- actually, what I want to say is page 2, there's my name as well. And it is true that I got this rank, but this is not my signature. So I really don't know whether this is in connection with the awarding of ranks or whether it's just like that, some kind of a forgery or whatever so that someone would know this or that. I really don't know. But what I do know is that this is not my signature. I can sign my name any number of times here for you, but this indeed is not my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's all I wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, very briefly. I have just a few questions while we're in open session and then just one question in private session. I don't want to harm the interests of the witness that the Prosecutor spoke of.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Vinac, a few minutes ago you explained that you were not a member of the Viteska Brigade. Tell us, please, once again, what was your duty at that time when you were wounded? Where did you work exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, at that time I worked in the military district of Vitez. I worked in the anti-aircraft defence in the department for air surveillance. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So in April 1993 you were one of the officers in the headquarters of Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: So by that very fact you did not belong to any other unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honours. From the very first day, I was in the Operative Zone of this area and I never worked in any other institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: One more question in this regard. You told the Honourable Judges yesterday and today that during the night you called the junior officer on duty in order to receive information about the situation because you had heard some rumours that had upset your neighbours in the afternoon. However, you did not say where this junior officer was on duty.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is true. The population was upset, so I called the junior officer on duty, because there were always two officers on duty. The senior officer on duty would work until 2400 hours, and after 2400 hours, the junior officer on duty would take over. It is true that I called the junior officer on duty, and I asked him about the situation in the zone of responsibility. That's exactly the way it was, and if necessary, I can give you the name of this junior officer who was on duty that night, but I think there is no need for that. So I received this information on the phone that everything was all right, that there were no problems whatsoever, and I went to bed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: All right. So this junior officer on duty was on duty at the headquarters that you worked in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That was at the hotel in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you. And just one more detail in connection with your wounding. Later, there were administrative things that were done in connection with your wounding; you had to attain certain rights, et cetera. Did you actually get to exercise these rights?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, no, because I had a salary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one minute in private session, please, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Vinac, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are released and free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you all as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the next witness is Josip Grubesic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let him be called. I'll have a word with the legal officer, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Grubesic, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I, Josip Grubesic, solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Would you please state your full name for the Court?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Josip Grubesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Grubesic, I'm going to take you very briefly through a number of preliminary pieces of information. It's true, is it not, that you were born on August the 31st, 1967, in the city of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You are a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and are a Bosnian Croat by ethnicity, and a Roman Catholic by religion; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe, Mr. Grubesic, that you currently live in Busovaca with your wife and daughter.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And since 1992, you have worked as a civilian policeman, and you're currently employed by the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, working at the police station in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, sir, let me turn your attention to January of 1993 and, specifically, January the 20 and or January the 21st. Were you a member of the escort accompanying Mr. Dario Kordic and Mr. Ignac Kostroman as they participated in talks with representatives of the SDA in either Travnik or Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I was one of the persons accompanying Mr. Kordic and Mr. Kostroman.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Grubesic, can you remember whether those talks were being held in Novi Travnik or Travnik or not?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: The talks were being held in Travnik at the building of the forestry administration. These were negotiations at party level between the HDZ and the SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And what happened after the talks were over?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: When the talks were over, we returned with our vehicles in the direction of Busovaca. Miro Musa, Mr. Kostroman and Ivo Arar were in one vehicle. In another vehicle was Mr. Kordic, escorted by Bogdan Santic, Milenko Arapovic and Damir Cosic. And in the third vehicle behind this one, that's where I was together with three other colleagues, civilian policemen. As we arrived in Busovaca, the vehicle of Mr. Kostroman continued in the direction of Kiseljak, while the other two vehicles turned towards the house of Mr. Kordic. Having arrived in front of Mr. Kordic's house, Mr. Kordic got out of the vehicle and entered the house. At that point in time, Bogdan Santic, his driver, who had a Motorola, that is to say that this is a walkie-talkie, heard that a checkpoint had been placed by what we call the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the area of Kacuni.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If I might interrupt you for just a second, is Mr. Kordic's house located in the eastern portion of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. If you could just resume your narrative to the Trial Chamber, Mr. Grubesic, about what you did after this Motorola or walkie-talkie message that was received by Mr. Santic.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Having received this message, Mr. Santic said to us, who were in the Renault 21, this other vehicle, to follow him to Kacuni because he thought that there could be some problems for Mr. Kostroman. He felt that he was in some kind of danger. We set off very fast in the direction of Kacuni. We were joined by yet another vehicle, an Ascona, where Dragan Vukadinovic was as well as Branislav Kristo. We came to a place where this checkpoint had been put. Actually, that is where the main road forks towards the Silos, and we saw anti-tank mines that had been placed there. On the left- and right-hand side, there was about 50 to 70 armed soldiers who pointed their weapons at us, and they ordered us to stop. I noticed the vehicle of Mr. Kostroman that had already been pulled over by the road leading to the Silos, and I noticed several soldiers with their weapons pointed at the persons in the vehicle. I also recognised --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: What kind of weapons, Mr. Grubesic, if I might just interrupt you? Sorry to do so.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Those were all automatic rifles, Kalashnikovs, 762 millimetres, and one person had a hand-held rocket launcher pointed at us, a rocket launcher for tanks, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And did you recognise the person who was pointing this shoulder-launched missile at the cars?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: A colleague who was with me in the vehicle warned me about this person and said that this was Miralem Delija. I had not known this individual from before, so this colleague of mine said, "This is Miralem Delija." After that --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Grubesic, in your statement, on paragraph 8, you say: "I recognised Miralem Delija." Is that correct or is that not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, just one moment, please. Mr. Sayers, that is a leading question. This is obviously important evidence and shouldn't be led. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Mr. President, and I did not mean to lead, and I apologise to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That was the effect of it, and then, of course, the difficulty is it then devalues the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Perhaps I can just let the Prosecution deal with that, as I'm sure that they will, and I'll just move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Grubesic, could you tell the Court what happened as this confrontation unfolded?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: We, who were in the vehicle, were ordered to remain in the vehicle and not to move. Bogdan Santic got out of his vehicle and discussed something with this person, Miralem Delija, who had this hand-held launcher pointed at us. At that point in time, an UNHCR convoy came up, or UNPROFOR; I'm not sure. They were white vehicles, vehicles marked white. So these persons who held weapons pointed at us were a bit perplexed. I felt that they didn't know what to do with us. So we took advantage of this opportunity, so to speak, and we proceeded, having gone round these mines that were placed on the road, and we continued towards Kiseljak. Bogdan Santic discussed something with these matters -- with these persons for about ten minutes, so when the convoy came, these persons didn't know what to do, and we took advantage of this opportunity and we left. We stopped, after two kilometres, by a cafe --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I don't mean to be discourteous, but matters of detail like that can be covered by the Prosecution, if they want. There's only one point that I want to raise with you, and that's as we think to be relevant here. Could you tell the Court whether Mr. Dario Kordic was involved in this incident at any point, whether he was there at any time during this confrontation that you've just described?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence of Mr. Cerkez has no questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What brigade were you a member of at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grubesic. The man said "Mr. Nice". That's how it was interpreted for me. The name is Mr. Grubesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, what brigade you were a member of?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the civilian police. I was not the member of a brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As a member of the civilian police, witnessing an event like this, you would no doubt have prepared a report?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I did not prepare a report then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you prepare a report at any stage?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did anyone from the Croat side prepare a report at any stage on this incident?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What records, if any, have you been able to refer before giving your evidence here today?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I did not have any notes available as far as this event is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When were you first asked to cast your mind back to these events in order that they might be written down?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: It was -- I think it was the month of January in the year 2000, I talked to the lawyer of Mr. Kordic in Busovaca. I think it was January. I can't say for sure now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When was your summary, which we've been provided a copy, first prepared in typed or written form?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you remember when you signed it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I signed it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Not the day before?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Or, actually, just a minute. Yesterday, yesterday -- no, the day before yesterday. You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: After the weekend, that's for sure?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When did you first recall any involvement of white vehicles that you say may have been UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I remember it. It was always in my mind. It is a very significant event in my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want to know if there's any document that you can point us to that will show that UNPROFOR must have observed this incident. You can think of no HVO record or civilian police record, can you, that would point to UNPROFOR's involvement?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Documents of the HVO or the civilian police? I cannot recall a civilian police document, but UNPROFOR made reports. They were very precise about things like that. They probably noted something down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you help us at all with who from UNPROFOR was involved or the nature of the vehicles in any more detail so that we can track down UNPROFOR and see if they can confirm what you say?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I cannot give you any details. There were about ten vehicles. As far as I can remember, there were UNPROFOR vehicles there and Red Cross vehicles there. And as for UNPROFOR reports, they register all their movements. They register all their movements. You can probably find this with them, to tell you the truth, at that time I didn't really pay much attention to this, because my life was in danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just this last detail on records at the moment. When were you first provided with a copy of a draft summary to look at?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Well, a few days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Inaudible]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think the answer was yes, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So to your knowledge, no written version of your summary existed before the weekend?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Help us, please, with how you put a date on this incident at all.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Well, I did not put a date on it. I cannot remember exactly whether it was the 20th of January or the 21st. It was one of those two days, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Seven years and more ago, to get it right within one or two days might not be that bad. How do you put it as either the 20th or the 21st, please?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I can tell you, I remember quite a number of dates from seven or eight years back, because that incident marked me. That was the first time that somebody pointed a firearm at my head, not one man, but more than 50 men, and one will remember that, won't one?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You don't, for example, link the incident to any other incident that happened on the same day and are able to give the date by that process?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I don't know what incident happened that day. On that day, as I told you, I think it was Travnik. But whether there was some incident, I don't know. I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You say that you passed on to Kiseljak; is that right? When did you return?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: No. Having passed the checkpoint, we stopped by a restaurant called Gazela, and there we spent quite some time discussing the situation that we found ourselves in. And after that -- it must have been after 6.00 in the afternoon, because it was getting dark -- and we saw Mr. Kostroman to Kresevo. And his driver, I don't know where he went, but we from the other two vehicles, we were around those cafes in Kresevo until after midnight. And then we went back to Busovaca and back home, I suppose; at least, I went home.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you heard nothing back at Busovaca that night, or the following day, about things that had happened on the day when you, as you say, had had a gun pointed at you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Apart from that incident, when we had arms pointing at us, no, I did not hear anything else happened that day. I told you: When we returned, I went straight home and fell asleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When, then, did you first hear about the death of Mirsad Delija?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I heard about that. I did not know straight away what that man's name was, but I heard about the incident and that a Bosniak had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I think it was perhaps two or three days after the incident on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you telling the Judges that for those intervening two or three days, nothing exceptional had happened in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Perhaps it did, but I don't know, because I spent at home during those two or three days. I was really under very severe stress, because that was the first time that I had firearms pointing at me. And it was only when I went to the police station, there was talk that some Delija had been killed, but I didn't know his first name at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The police records may show, if they exist, that you were at home with stress-related illness for those two or three days; is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: It wasn't an illness, and whether there are any documents about that, I really don't know, I mean, that I was at home. My wife can confirm it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You may or may not have been at home, but you were, I think, a member of the armed guard for Kordic and Kostroman; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I was, on behalf of the civilian police, one who was an escort, not a guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And in the nature of things, escorts, or guards, are likely to come up against unpleasant situations, but are you really telling us the situation kept you off work for days so that you didn't learn about what was happening in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I already told you: That day, when I returned to Busovaca, or rather that night, I went home. And after -- and I cannot really say for sure 100 per cent -- after some time I heard that Delija had been killed. But I heard about that incident. All sorts of rumours circulated around the town about that incident. There were different versions of it, but, believe me, I didn't really pay much attention to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You better tell us so that we have a complete picture. What rumours do you say were circulating?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Well, there were rumours circulating that Delija had been killed by some masked individuals. There was another story around that he wanted to throw a bomb, a grenade at somebody. There were different versions. But at that time I was not on the investigating team, so that I really wasn't interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You said something, when a proposition was put to you, about recognising somebody in a car. Now, let's hear it from you. Who was it that you were able to recognise in a car?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: What car?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the checkpoint. Somebody with an RPG-7, it said. Who were you able to recognise?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes. When we arrived at the checkpoint, we saw that individual with this RPG pointing, and one of the colleagues who was with me in the car said that that was Miralem Delija.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. Until then you didn't know him?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At all?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: At all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It would, of course, be quite wrong to say that you recognised somebody who you didn't know, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I did not know him before, and at that moment, when he pointed the RPG at me, I saw him very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And that was really seeing him for the first time?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And I expect -- well, you haven't seen him since?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Since that event, you mean? Since that event, I never saw him again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you explain to us, please, how you were able to sign a statement -- no doubt it's in your own language, but as translated into English, if accurately translated, it reads -- at this point of your narrative, it reads: "Among them, I recognised Miralem Delija." Do take your original version from your pocket, if that's where it is, and look at it, or I'm sure that the lawyers will provide you with one in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I don't have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Here comes one from Mr. Naumovski.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I don't have it. You don't have to give me the version. There is no need for it. According to me, it changes nothing insofar as the incident itself is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may not, Mr. Grubesic, but these documents -- this document is presented as a version of events that you have signed as accurate. Now, look at paragraph 8, which you must have read, in this short two-page document. Does it say, in the second sentence of paragraph 8: "Among them, I recognised Miralem Delija"?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: There is, but this is just a framework, subject to further discussion. You said yourself this is just a draft.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, I did not say that. I asked you if there was an earlier draft. This is presented as the final version, signed by you.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: There was no earlier version.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I may return to that. Miralem Delija conducted some inquiries of his own in your area before he was killed in entirely separate circumstances. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: No. I don't even know that he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Akrap Spomenko, was he present with you at the time of this incident?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know that individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you know somebody by the name of Puljik Zarko?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: There are several of them in Busovaca, in Busovaca alone. I don't know which one do you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you know somebody by the name of Relota Brane?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I know three Brane Relotas in Busovaca alone, and I know all three of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was one person with that name with you at the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then finally, for this purpose, Dragan Vukadinovic, was he with you at the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: A Dragan Vukadinovic was, but there's also quite a number of them in the town too, four or five of them. I'd need some particulars.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who was it of the people in the cars, or car, that gave you the name of Miralem Delija, please?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Milijan Kristo. He told me. He came from Kacuni and he lived in Kacuni, in the area of Kacuni, up there, and presumably he knew those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is it the case that you, with Zarko Puljic, Brane Relota, and Dragan Vukadinovic, visited the home of Miralem Delija later that same evening?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I don't know where Miralem Delija's home is, and we did not visit it, because I told you that Brane -- what did you say he was? Brane Relota, is it? He wasn't at the checkpoint with me, so I really don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether, after the checkpoint incident, you, with others, visited the home of what was certainly thought to be the family of Miralem Delija. Did you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I've already told you. After we went through the checkpoint, we went to Gazela, the restaurant. We spent there some time and then we went to Kresevo. I think I was quite clear about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm suggesting -- I'm asking, not suggesting; I'm asking whether you, in fact, knew rather more about the killing because you were present when it happened, the killing not, of course, of Miralem, but of his brother, who by chance was there.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I was not present and I cannot tell you anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's go back to the beginning. If we can think of the road running between Busovaca and Kiseljak as north/south -- it's not north/south, but conceptually think of it as north/south -- if you were coming from Travnik going to Kiseljak, you would be travelling north/south; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Travnik. Well, I wouldn't really say so. It doesn't look like that on the map. But you said to simplify matters, and if we are simplifying matters, then yes, we can say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Coming from other places, simply, for example, Fojnica, going to Busovaca, you would pass the same point in the road but you would be travelling north?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: No. Going from Fojnica to Busovaca, you go from the opposite direction, completely opposite than the one from Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: They are two different directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Exactly. You would travel on the same road but in the opposite direction if, for example, you were coming from Fojnica?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. No, not from Fojnica. From Fojnica, to reach that road, you have to take another road, because there is a separate road taking you to Fojnica. The one that we're referring to is Kaonik-Blazuj high road, and when you go to Fojnica, you have to change to a different road which is 12 kilometres long, and it is that other road that you can get to Fojnica by. That is not the same road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We may have to look at the map a little later. But you were on escort duty this day -- and Fojnica we can disregard for the time being. You were on escort duty on this day, and the only place where you went to for a meeting was Travnik, was it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Yes, and Kresevo on our way back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Had you been doing escort duties earlier this same week; the previous day, for example?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I think not. I did escort Mr. Kordic on several other occasions, but that particular week, I can't really recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But this Travnik meeting was the only meeting that you can tell us about because it was the only meeting that you knew of?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: No. I knew about some other meetings, too, when I was present escorting Mr. Kordic. Well, sometimes he went to Vitez, sometimes he went to Kiseljak, sometimes down to Herzegovina, at times to Zenica, also went to Zenica. There were those meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At this time that you remember, these two days, the 20th/21st of January, the only meeting that you can recall is the meeting in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Now, yes, at the moment the only one that I really recall being among the escort was that one, because what happened after that, after we left Travnik, was quite specific. I'm referring to the incidents at the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who did you meet in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I did not meet anyone. What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who did Mr. Kordic --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Can you clarify?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who were you going there to meet?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: We -- well, the escorts were usually outside the building, waiting for those meetings to be over. What they talk about at those meetings, we don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, can you give us a clue as to who was involved? It was the representatives, I think, of -- well, you tell us. Who was it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, it was an HDZ meeting of the political party and the SDA. I remember Mr. Kordic was there, Mr. Kostroman, and others. As for the Bosniak side, well, I don't really know them very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But this was a political meeting between the SDA and the HDZ. You've seen no record to show that this meeting occurred, have you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to suggest to you, until such time as I'm shown a document to prove otherwise, that there was indeed no such meeting in Travnik or Novi Travnik between these two political groups on either the 20th or the 21st of January and that what you've told us about that is completely incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Well, you should ask that -- you should ask that -- about that to those who attended the meeting. I know where I went that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness see, please, Exhibit 384A.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's no possibility, is there, of a meeting having occurred on either -- on the day you were escorting Mr. Kordic, there's no possibility of a meeting happening in Fojnica, is there, just to clarify the position, because you'd have known about it? Is there?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: No, I don't think I would be in a position to know. I wasn't the only one who provided escort. There were different -- a number of policemen who provided the escort.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You weren't in Fojnica, were you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Not on any one of those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. You see, this is a document. I don't suggest you would have seen it before, but it's apparently a document from --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Let me just read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course. I'll just explain it, to make it easier for you. It's dated the 21st of January, and it's going to Mostar from Mr. Kvesic, but it says this: "On the 20th of January of 1993, a meeting was held in Fojnica with Mijat Tuka, the president of the Fojnica HVO," other people are listed, and then we come to "Mr. Ignac Kostroman and Mr. Dario Kordic." Does that help you at all with where you were?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this document, it does not say that Mr. Kordic was there. The question that was asked was not precise. That might confuse him. What it says here, that the meeting was held at the order of Mr. Ignac Kostroman and Mr. Kordic. So a meeting was held and they discussed about something, but the meeting was convened upon the orders from Ignac Kostroman and Dario Kordic, not that they were there. Let us try not to confuse the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, in the next paragraph, it says: "A proposal was put forward by Messrs. Kordic and Kostroman to appoint Perica." Is that the passage you rely on, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It certainly is, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. What do you say about this, Mr. Grubesic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I cannot say anything about this document. This is the first time I see it, and I was not in Fojnica on those two days. I was -- on the 20th or the 21st of January, I was escorting Mr. Kordic and Mr. Kostroman to Travnik, and these are the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You know, do you, that the evidence given thus far about this incident is to the effect that the convoy was indeed travelling using the way I described it, south-north, consistent with coming from Fojnica; you know that's the evidence so far, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: The convoy which arrived at that checkpoint cannot be said to have arrived from Fojnica, because from that place you cannot see the road to Fojnica. You could ask me if it arrived from the direction of Kiseljak or maybe Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Using the simple conceptual approach I invited you to adopt, you know, don't you, that the evidence thus far given in this court about this checkpoint incident is that the small convoy of vehicles was stopped travelling from the south to the north; you know that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Which small convoy of vehicles? You were not precise enough. Do you mean UNPROFOR vehicles or do you mean our vehicles?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your vehicles.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: We travelled from Busovaca in the direction -- from the direction of Busovaca in the direction of Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You haven't answered my last question, but I'll move to the next one. You also know that travelling conceptually south-north, you would not have passed Busovaca by the time you reached the checkpoint, and therefore it would not have been possible for Mr. Kordic to have left the vehicle to go home, and that is the reason why you are saying -- and it may be other witnesses -- that you are saying the convoy came from the north and went south; you're saying that in order to give a possible explanation for Kordic leaving the car in Busovaca, and what you've told us is quite untrue?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I did not -- I did not say from what direction the convoy came. I said that the convoy passed while we were at the checkpoint, the convoy passed through. And your concepts about north and south, south-north, if you gave me a map, then I would find my way about it. But you are saying that you want to simplify matters, but I think you are making things more intricate, because you are not defining what is north, what is south, what is south, what is north. On the map, I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps we'll deal with it by a map after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But what I'm going to press you on just at this stage is this: The alleged meeting in Travnik or Novi Travnik that you are describing is something that, again, unless I'm shown a document, you've had to create in order to give a possibility for Kordic to have got out of the car before he reached -- before the other cars reached the checkpoint; isn't that the truth?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: No, it is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll adjourn now. Mr. Grubesic, will you remember, during the adjournment, not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and of course don't let anybody speak to you about it, and that does include the Defence lawyers. Yes, Mr. Naumovski. Are you merely early for rising, or is there a point you want to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, just one minute, if I may. Your Honours, we planned another witness for today, Mr. Arar, who was to come immediately after Mr. Grubesic. However, the Registry has just notified us that Mr. Arar has ended up in hospital. He has a stomach ulcer and seems to have left his medicines behind -- we don't really know -- so that we do not think that somehow -- it seems that he won't be able to attend before the Court today. Another witness that we had planned for this week arrived yesterday, late in the evening. We never talked to him before, so we shall have to talk to him this afternoon, and he would be ready tomorrow morning. Of course, if Mr. Arar is well enough and ready, then he will also appear. So, unfortunately, after this witness we shall not have any other witness. This was merely to inform the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll see what the position is when this witness finishes. There is one matter which is outstanding, and that concerns the witness list for Mr. Cerkez. Mr. Mikulicic, it may be convenient at some stage today to discuss that. Maybe after this witness. We'll see how things go. We'll adjourn for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, for a map, we probably can't do better than 2612.2, given the towns to be covered. If the usher could just hand it to me, I'll open it at the place that -- or try and compose it in such a way that it covers the relevant areas. Inevitably, it will be a fold on the map, as it always is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, take your time to familiarise yourself with this map, and it may be that the bend in it can be flattened out a little bit by the usher. Can you see there, first of all, Kacuni, and just point that out with the pointer you'll be given. There's Busovaca under your finger. And to the right of that, we come to Kacuni. There we are. Now, if we can look further down on the map we can see Fojnica. Just point that out for us, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think the usher will have to move the map a little just so that we can be sure we all see it. Thank you. Fojnica is further down. Further down still, I think. Keep going. Thank you. There's Fojnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, to reach Kacuni from Fojnica, if you take the main road, you'd take the road travelling east and then you'd turn left and bear north-west. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One way or the other, coming from Fojnica, you would approach Kacuni from -- I've called it the south, but it's really the south-east -- and you reach Kacuni before you reach Busovaca. That's the simple point and that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: When you go from Fojnica, you go east, to the M5 road, Kaonik-Blazuj, and then you turn to the left. Kiseljak is on the right. And you go left to return to Busovaca, so that's the road [indicating].

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And coming from Travnik, or Novi Travnik, as you've already explained, you come in the opposite direction. That's all I need on that. Thank you very much. As to the incident itself, can I just ask you this, please: Are you telling us that while you were still looking after Mr. Kordic, you heard something or somebody heard something over a walkie-talkie?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: No. Mr. Kordic had already entered the house. When Bogdan Santic heard that something was going on, he heard that in the walkie-talkie. Bogdan Santic told us that in Kacuni some kind of a checkpoint had been erected. Mr. Kordic didn't even know about that, because he had already entered the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were on police duty, but how were you dressed, or can't you remember?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: I remember. I had a military uniform, a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll come back to that again later. But you would have had information that was available generally to the HVO about checkpoints and matters of that sort, wouldn't you? It would be necessary to know where checkpoints were to do your job of escorting important people around?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: You know what? At that time, anybody could have placed a checkpoint, so it was very difficult to know where and when there was a checkpoint. Those were times of total anarchy, and anybody could go out into the road, armed, and place a checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Nakic has told us that he was aware of the existence of this checkpoint as early as the 19th of January. Mr. Nakic's information would have been shared with you, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know what Mr. Nakic knew. I'm just talking from my own point of view. I found out about the checkpoint when I saw it. But we heard about it -- or rather Bogdan heard about it over the walkie-talkie a few minutes earlier, and then he told us, from the vehicle, about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you saying that he heard that there was an incident involving Mr. Kostroman or simply that there was going to be a checkpoint that Mr. Kostroman would have to pass? Which is it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: He simply told us, "It seems that there is a checkpoint in Kacuni. There are people who are armed there. Kostroman went off to Kiseljak. Let's go and find out what's happening." Those are the words he used. And we set off from Mr. Kordic's house in the direction of Kacuni. We passed through the centre of the town of Busovaca at great speed, and we went towards Kacuni.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Again, I'm going to suggest to you that your account of this conversation by Bogdan Santic on the radio or the telephone is something that's explained or -- is designed to explain away your presence there at all and that it is not true.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: But it is true. I was there, I was present there, and I know the best how it exactly happened. Only a few words can differ from the original story. I cannot remember each and every word, but that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You arrived coming from probably Fojnica or that direction?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: No. We came from the direction of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were in plain clothes yourself, and you were in the first car?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: No. I was in the third car in the motorcade, and I had a military camouflage uniform on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The fourth vehicle contained one of the men, Vukadinovic, and the man you say you don't know, Spomenko Akrap, but did you know a man going by the name of Carli?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: No, no. No, no, no, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It was you who were abusive to Miralem, the man you say was pointed out to you, when he asked for some identity from the driver of your car?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: In the fourth car was Dragan Vukadinovic and not a person I did not know. There was another person I knew. That was Branko Branislav Kristo. And you mentioned this abuse of Miralem Delija. That's ridiculous. When 50 people are holding you at gunpoint, you are only in a position to beg and plead with someone, not to abuse them. Had we abused anyone, we would have been killed. One could even hear shouts of, "Kill them, kill them," but they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your suggestion of the number of people there is an exaggeration. There's only probably some 15 or 20, as the independent international observers record it at the time, and that the figure of 70 is an exaggeration.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: No. I said "from 50 to 70," 70 rather than 50, because on the left side and on the right side, there were a lot of armed men. There were sandbags there also, and behind them were armed men. Some were laying on the grass, and others were standing. At any rate, it was a very unpleasant situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you were disarmed by the Muslims, and Kordic reacted to that; isn't that what happened?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Kordic could not have reacted. Kordic had stayed at home. The Muslims did not disarm us; they just said that we shouldn't move, move out of the cars, that is. The Muslims disarmed the vehicle where Kostroman was. I know that a rifle was taken out of Mr. Kostroman's car, and a pistol too. We were not disarmed. At that moment, from the direction of Kiseljak came this convoy of UNPROFOR or UNHCR; I can't say for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness see Exhibit 461, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you telling us, incidentally, that on your return from Kiseljak later that night, you had no problems at the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: We were not returning to Kiseljak. We went to Kresevo, and on our way back, we did not find anyone at that place where the checkpoint was. There wasn't anyone there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we ought to go into private session. This document is confidential.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't want to take a bad point against you, but I must just ask you this: Is your account of the alleged -- not involvement, but significance of UNPROFOR, who you say turned up to save the day, is your account of that built on the fact that a witness gave evidence about UNPROFOR last week, that you're simply reflecting evidence that you know has been given by another witness?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: You know what? I do not know who testified or what he testified about, and UNPROFOR or UNHCR did not turn up there to save the situation. They simply happened to turn up, and we used that to -- we seized upon it to somehow get out of the predicament.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With there being some 70 armed men, you were able to run away, were you, get away?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP GRUBESIC
utterances.text: Well, Bogdan Santic was negotiating with those soldiers, and I suppose when he started in his vehicle, we were in our vehicle. But when Bogdan started his vehicle and when Kostroman left, then we simply followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nothing else. There's another document that touches on the incident of the 20th of January meeting, which, for completeness, you may like to have referred to, and that is -- it's 386A, and it's a document of the 21st of January which confirms the appointment of the man referred to, Nikola Perica, in the middle of Exhibit 384A. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No questions on direct, Your Honour, but we would simply draw the Court's attention to Exhibit D152/1, page 27, the commander's diary of the 1st Cheshires, which makes a reference to four separate convoys that proceeded on that day, one from Zenica to Kiseljak. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Give me that exhibit number again. 152/1?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Page?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Page 27, I believe. Let me just check that. Yes, 27, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Grubesic, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Naumovski, have you any more news?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, Your Honours, I have no news. The last thing we heard is that Mr. Arar, our next witness, had been taken to the hospital because he was in severe pain last night, and this morning was taken to the hospital. He had nobody to turn to during the night, so that it happened this morning. I understand it is nothing life-threatening, that this is his regular complaint. But if he spends -- if he can have some rest this afternoon, because last night he went without sleep, then I suppose he'll be all right to come and testify tomorrow morning. But that is only my estimate. The other witness has arrived, is in The Hague, and will be ready for tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If we did adjourn until tomorrow, could we hear both witnesses during the course of the day? Is there any problem about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] None whatsoever. There will be plenty of time for both witnesses. One of them is very short, and the other one won't be anything special. So I'm positive that we shall be able to finish them tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're in touch with the Victims and Witnesses Unit, are you, about the one who's in hospital?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And that is the news that you have, that he's there. Well, if at all possible, he should be --

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues]... because it will be a waste of time if he's come here to no effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed, we shall do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn the evidence until tomorrow. But we have some minutes before the adjournment. There are one or two matters we want to deal with. The first is to review progress with the Kordic Defence team; secondly, to deal with the Cerkez Defence and witnesses; and, thirdly, there's a matter which we want to raise with the Prosecution ex parte, if there's time to do that. Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm happy to say that we remain on schedule, notwithstanding the extraordinary amount of time that the cross-examination is taking. We abide by the estimate that we've previously provided to the Court. We hope to be finished by the August break, and as I said I think twice earlier, sometime before that, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've given -- I have got myself -- I don't think my colleagues have seen -- your batting order for the next two weeks: eight witnesses for next week, and six for the week after.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: On the second week, Your Honour, if I might add, there may be some additional witnesses. We haven't had the opportunity to consult with them yet. Six seems rather light, given the fact that that's a full week, and we're aware of that and we'll try to keep the week filled with evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We've got a Chambers day one afternoon there, but these are all relatively short witnesses, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If I can go down the list, Your Honour, the first witness should be fairly short; the second witness, perhaps a little longer; the third witness, very short. The fourth witness gives evidence about Kakanj, and he should be relatively short. The fifth witness is a Croat victim who provides evidence about Kakanj. She'll be extremely short. The sixth witness provides evidence about Travnik. The seventh witness provides evidence about a witness who has testified. And the last witness is a representative of TV Vitez, and the testimony there will be very short. For the week after, I won't say the name, but the Court will notice that that is someone who was referred to today. We do not anticipate that this evidence will be particularly long. The second witness will be very short. The third witness will be one of the witnesses who gives evidence about Busovaca, our first witness, and a prominent politician, and his testimony could be fairly substantial. The fourth witness for the second week, relatively short. The fifth witness is obviously a substantial witness from Busovaca, and then the last witness is a short witness. So it may be that the witnesses in the order that we've listed, and those specific names, would actually consume both full weeks, now that I look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I calculate that we have something of the order of 47 to 48 sitting days before the recess, so that's nearly nine weeks, and I hope that will be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I do too, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. At some stage we will have a look again, perhaps in two weeks' time, at your original list, and it may be you can help us by going through, showing the ones which you now do not intend or will not be in a position to call.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'm happy to do that, Mr. President. I'm sure it won't have escaped the Trial Chamber's notice that many of the witnesses listed have submitted affidavits, and therefore economies are produced in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Mr. Kovacic, you've been asked to justify the length of your witness list because of its extensive nature, well over a hundred. In fact, 147 names appear on it. Now, in my judgement, such a list is not reasonable. I know that you say, in relation to it, that this is a list of all possible witnesses, and you don't intend to call them all, and in fact, you think that the likely number is going to be somewhere in the region of 60 or so. But in order for us to be able to arrange our work, we need to know, with more certainty, what the reality of the position is. I notice, for instance, the list includes two of the accused before this Tribunal. Is it really suggested that they are going to give evidence? Does this represent, as it were, a wish list, what you would wish in the best of all possible worlds, or does it represent a more realistic list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yes, I understand your question, and I understand your concern. If I may remind you, the same kind of questions were asked of Mr. Kordic's Defence before I planned my list, because I had the privilege of doing it at a later date. Needless to say, I did have in mind these questions even before I submitted this list. But I should like to go back to it now. You asked -- yes, you are quite right, it is the list of our wishes rather. Secondly, in view of the restrictions or, rather, instructions you issued to us, we submitted our list of witnesses, bearing in mind that more is less, and we think that this list of witnesses, plus some definitions, are a data bank, and from it we intend to draw what seems relevant to us or what will seem relevant to us when our turn comes. We believe -- and the further we proceed in this case and the more we become acquainted with Mr. Kordic's Defence, because certain things may overlap -- it seems to us today that, objectively speaking, we could bring in, for direct evidence, something about 50 witnesses; perhaps a little less than 50, but it is difficult for me to say so now. One of the chief unknowns is that some of the incidents overlap and that Mr. Kordic's Defence -- we have already heard, for instance, a great deal of evidence regarding counts 1 and 2 of the indictment; that is, insofar as my client is concerned, count 2, and that is persecution. So I had already stricken out some witnesses on my list, because evidently some of the facts have now become quite clear through this other Defence and I do not have to repeat it. Secondly, from this list we shall single out a certain number, and I shall say today that there will be something like 20, 25 individuals. We shall single them out, and their testimonies, because these are only minor details corroborating the facts, and we shall offer them as affidavits obtained under the Bosnian laws and under the Rules of this Tribunal. This mechanism was owing to the positive attitude of the BH ministry, which has finally been established and now is beginning to work. We did not know about that before, but now it seems that this mechanism is quite all right and can be used. Thirdly, transcript witnesses from other cases, I am envisaging some 20, I believe, that we shall be introducing from other cases. And in this manner, we shall again be cutting short the need for their physical appearance before this Court. And finally, we have another group which was in a different category, and I cannot now quote them, simply out of some caution, because I do see them on Mr. Kordic's list, but I do not know whether they will be appearing or not. So if they come to testify in Mr. Kordic's case, then, needless to say, I will not be calling them again. I should also like to suggest that in two or three weeks' time, we perhaps give you an update of the state of affairs as we move on in Mr. Kordic's case. That is, I am suggesting I am planning to do that regardless of whether you will order me to do so or not. I should like to seize this opportunity to ask you, Your Honours, in view of two accused, certain things seem to be duplicated, and it will help me not to have to produce some evidence on counts 1 and 2, that is, persecution, because there the evidence is common, more or less, except that I will have to perhaps devote more attention to two or three details which have to do with Vitez. But again I will have to see what Mr. Kordic's Defence will do. But the offence is qualified identically, the largest number of exhibits go to that. And then also as to the matter of international armed conflict, again we have an almost identical situation, and I do not think that we have to single out Vitez, as such. And there is quite a lot of evidence about this, so that will be that. Two persons who are in The Hague here, having been accused and are in the Detention Unit now, who are on my list, we thought, and I think now, that we could resolve it with affidavits, because in the case of those two witnesses, I had in mind two facts that they were restricted to; not their testimony about their whole story, because that would be impossible and it would be conflicting with their interests and there would be a conflict of interest, and I really did not want to go into that area, into that grey area. I can tell you what it is about, but I do not think it is necessary to do so. In both those cases, it is simply a fact, an event. And this is 15 minutes' worth of testimony so far as direct examination would be concerned, so something that would be resolved by way of affidavit. But in a way, I do have to bring in a witness who will provide a link with this corroborative testimony. By "corroborative", I mean the two persons accused before this Tribunal. If you want me to say what it is, that one of them is mentioned regarding the murder in the motel, that he was there as the chief of the military police in the Territorial Defence. He was escorting then Commander Hasan Cengic, and that was said by a witness that we heard here. And it was asserted today that Mr. Cerkez, who was wearing a black uniform, was surrounded by bodyguards in black uniforms. I thought of calling this witness only to confirm whether he was, indeed, one of the escorts of the TO, whether he saw Cerkez, and whether he was there. So three or four questions, not more than 10 minutes altogether. But I can, of course, obtain an affidavit from him, since he is in the Netherlands. Under the Dutch law, we have already had a statement produced pursuant to the Dutch law, and perhaps that could be a way to do it. That is one minor detail. And to conclude, as far as my case is concerned, unfortunately, of course, I am aware that perhaps our plans are very extensive at the moment, but I should like to remind the Court that in some cases, even after almost a year of the Prosecution's case, we still fail to understand some of the exhibits, what count of the indictment they refer to, what is it to, and whether we, indeed, need to provide any exhibits, especially insofar as character testimony is concerned. That is, whenever Mr. Cerkez is mentioned, even when a Prosecution witness has mentioned him in the struggle against the Serbs, and where it has to do with our motions for the rejection of the indictment, even that is placed within a bad context, because it seems as if the Prosecution believes that the struggle against the Serbs was also serving the persecution or whatever. And in that case, of course, I shall have to show the situation and the aspect. So it is those minor characterising details which should serve to come to a general conclusion of Mr. Cerkez, I think serve no other purpose but obfuscation of the whole situation, and, of course, they have to respond to that. Fortunately, on the other hand, these are brief testimonies. These are witnesses of whom we shall have only a few questions to ask, and I do not think they will have too much time. Needless to say, I shall be very happy to answer any question, or perhaps even, if you want me, I can attempt to assess the time, if you wish me to do so, although I think it is a little premature to do so. But if I look at the pace at which Mr. Kordic's Defence is progressing, and having in mind the structure of long and short witnesses, that is, those who will take a lot of time or those who will take very little time, I think we could move on at a rate of some six to seven witnesses per week. And if we therefore are dealing with some 50 witnesses, more or less, I believe that some eight working weeks could suffice. I also believe that the Prosecution will cross-examine them within reasonable limits of time, not more than twice as long as the Defence. That is, if we examine a witness for about an hour, then he should not spend more than three hours in the courtroom. I think it is even beyond physical endurance. I mean on the average, of course. Therefore, I believe that eight weeks should do it, of course with a considerable number of affidavits and evidence by transcript, as I have said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kovacic. That is clear. We would encourage you to keep us updated with progress regularly. We shall, of course, have to have a full Defence Status Conference before you begin your Defence, at some stage towards the end of the Kordic Defence. Meanwhile, we would encourage you to proceed by affidavit and transcript. One detail. You talk of 20 or so transcript witnesses. The earlier you could get those before the Trial Chamber, the better, in case there are objections, and we could then rule upon them and, in that way, expedite matters, and indeed any other evidence as you can get before us before then in one way or another, we would encourage you to do. Thank you very much. Now, unless there's anything that anybody wants to raise -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A small matter. The transcript in the Prosecution case, the Court will remember that His Honour Judge Bennouna asked if we could identify the passages upon which we particularly relied, and in accordance with that request, we marked the pages, at the side of them, with lines as to the passages that we would particularly invite you to rely on. We didn't do it on officially paginated pages of the Registry version of the transcript. It was a very large exercise. We've been asked now to repeat the exercise with official pages. In all transcripts bar, I think, six or seven, in fact, the page numbers already provided are exactly the same as on the official page numbers of the institution, and we would ask that the existing documents could be accepted by the Chamber. It's a very large task to replicate the markings on these pages, and we frankly don't have to resources at the moment to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll look at that. Very well. Unless there's anything else, we'll adjourn the proceedings in open court until 9.30 tomorrow. Let me just make an inquiry of the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We shall sit again ex parte in ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: at 12.32 p.m. to be followed by an ex parte hearing.
